title: Cassiopeia A - The colorful aftermath of a violent stellar death
caption: Cassiopeia A supernova remnant, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Cassiopeia A, SN 1680 · constellation Cassiopeia · about 11000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and the Hubble Heritage (STScI/AURA)-ESA/Hubble Collaboration. Acknowledgement: Robert A. Fesen (Dartmouth College, USA) and James Long (ESA/Hubble)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Hubble view shows the tattered wreckage of a star that blew itself apart. The remnant is called Cassiopeia A, or Cas A for short, and it lies about 11,000 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia.

A supernova remnant is the expanding cloud of debris left behind when a massive star explodes. Cas A is the youngest known remnant of such an explosion in our own galaxy, the Milky Way. It is also cataloged as SN 1680.

Hubble's sharp eye picks out how complicated that debris is. Rather than forming a smooth, simple shell, the shattered fragments of the star make up a complex and intricate structure. The picture was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using three filters that record red and near-infrared light.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (8.55 x 6.15 arcminutes) and distance (11000 light years), the frame spans roughly 27 × 20 light-years. Its light set out about 11,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys recorded this image through red and near-infrared filters. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the light used here is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the long exposures reveal debris far too faint to see directly.

explore: The remnant is cataloged both as Cassiopeia A, named for the constellation in which it appears, and as SN 1680. The Hubble picture comes from the Advanced Camera for Surveys.
alt: The shattered, intricately structured remains of an exploded star.
